analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run public health insurance plan sold alongside private plans on the ACA exchanges.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2017 with 9 House sponsors, all Democrats, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to offer its own health insurance plan through the ACA exchanges, starting in 2018. The public plan would pay doctors and hospitals at Medicare rates, at least initially, and would be required to keep premiums low enough to cover its own costs. The goal was to give people a cheaper alternative to private insurance and force private insurers to compete on price.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying coverage on the ACA exchanges would gain a new, government-backed option that the bill requires to be designed as a low-cost plan, paying providers at Medicare rates, which are typically lower than private insurance rates. People in areas with few insurers would gain another choice. Taxpayers were protected in the design: the plan's premiums had to fully cover its costs, and a one-time $2 billion startup appropriation had to be repaid to the Treasury over 10 years.

how_it_helps.text: HHS would be required to offer a public plan through the exchanges whose 'primary responsibility is to create a low-cost plan without compromising quality or access to care.'
The plan would pay doctors and hospitals at Medicare rates for its first three years, with a 5% bonus for participating practitioners, and an ombudsman office would handle enrollees' complaints.

Premiums would be geographically adjusted but set only at a level sufficient to fully finance the plan's benefits, administrative costs, and a contingency margin, and the $2 billion startup funding would be repaid over 10 years.
Providers participating in Medicare would automatically be in the plan's network unless they opted out, which would help ensure people using the plan could find a doctor.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a government competitor selling on the same exchanges, potentially taking away enrollment. Hospitals and providers would be paid Medicare rates rather than higher private-insurance rates for patients on the plan, and would have to opt out affirmatively to stay out of its network. The plan itself would receive a $2 billion federal startup appropriation and 90 days of claims reserves, repaid over a decade.

drawbacks.text: Critics of Medicare-rate-based public options argue that paying providers at Medicare rates can push costs onto private payers or squeeze rural hospitals that rely on higher private reimbursement; the bill mitigated this with 5% higher payment rates for practitioners during the first three years.

The startup appropriation of $2 billion plus 90 days of claims reserves is a real federal outlay, even though the bill requires it to be amortized and repaid to the Treasury over 10 years and bars any additional appropriations to the plan.
The bill allows the Secretary to limit judicial and administrative review of the payment rates it sets, which reduces outside checks on how those rates are calculated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people struggling with exchange premiums, the bill offered a concrete alternative: a plan required to be low-cost, self-financing after startup, and paying providers at Medicare rates. The main honest concerns are that Medicare-level rates could shift costs or strain hospitals in some regions, and the $2 billion startup is real money, though it was designed to be repaid. The design aimed for deficit neutrality, as its own title ('Deficit Reduction Act') signals. It never advanced far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, then sent to the Health Subcommittee two weeks later, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2019 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio, joined by Rep. Steve Cohen, introduced the bill on March 2, 2017.
The same day it was introduced, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On March 17, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 115th Congress.
Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and hospitals that would have faced Medicare-rate competition on the exchanges are better off, since the bill never got a hearing or vote in committee.

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a public health insurance option paying providers at Medicare rates.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Joined DeFazio as the bill's other original sponsor at introduction.

for.name: 8 of 8 cosponsors (House Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all eight cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Rep. Greg Walden
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on March 17, 2017 and never held a hearing or markup on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for floor action; it never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Democrats, and with a Republican House majority the bill stayed in committee; no Republican support appears anywhere in the record.

industries.note: A government plan on the same exchanges, required to be low-cost and financed by its own premiums, would compete directly for the customers private insurers now serve on the exchanges. Insurers' interest in keeping this alternative off the table runs against exchange shoppers looking for cheaper coverage.

The plan would pay hospitals at Medicare rates, which are generally lower than private-insurance rates, and hospitals in Medicare would be in its network unless they opted out. Hospitals that bill private insurers at higher margins had a direct financial stake in the bill not advancing.

Doctors on the plan would be paid at Medicare rates, but the bill offered 5% higher rates for the first three years to draw participation, and providers could decline participation annually. Physicians' groups generally oppose Medicare-rate expansion, while the payment floor and ombudsman protections cushioned enrollees.
For drugs not covered under Medicare Part A or B, the Secretary would pay rates the Secretary negotiates, rather than the prices drugmakers charge private plans.
